Your Training Path

The primary path now contains 41 focused training lessons. Repeat, pause, or revisit skills as your dog needs — lesson numbers are a learning sequence, not calendar deadlines.

How to use this path: Learn lessons explain only the decisions you need before practice. Practice lessons build one skill in an easy setup. Field Sessions apply skills outside. During trigger work, judge whether the setup is workable, use the full Exposure Difficulty Map rather than distance alone, and progress from trends across sessions — not because the next lesson or the calendar says to make things harder.

I’m Stuck — Troubleshooting

Start with what you are actually seeing. You do not need to know which lesson contains the answer.

Safety first. If you cannot physically control your dog, there is meaningful bite or redirected-aggression risk, your dog may escape, or you feel unsafe, stop the training setup and seek individualized professional help. Sudden or substantial behaviour change can also warrant veterinary assessment.

Search everything

Use ordinary language: “staring,” “won’t eat,” “worked at home,” “reacted,” “too close,” “recovery,” or “which tool.”

Progress & Feedback

Track changes that matter in real life — not just lessons completed, distance, or whether barking happened.

Measure function, not a perfect score

A useful snapshot asks whether your dog can disengage, move and explore, recover, and make useful choices — and whether you are noticing earlier and choosing a response that fits the situation. Compare similar situations when possible. A harder environment can produce a harder snapshot without meaning the training is going backward.
